extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and fact-checkers interested in satirical and fake-news websites
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia list enumerating websites described by journalists, fact-checkers, and researchers as satirical or fake‑news sources, and summarizing signals and behaviors used to classify them (disclaimers, networks, deceptive practices, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a disclaimer labeling content as satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though many satirical sources are labeled as such with disclaimers, there is a long history of satirical content being falsely perceived as true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites multiple examples where sites include explicit disclaimers (e.g., 'All news articles contained within National Report are fiction', 'satirical site designed to parody the 24-hour news cycle'). Note that some sites have visible disclaimers while others have hidden or obscure disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden or obscure disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some webpages include a hidden disclaimer that claims itself as satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hidden or hard-to-find disclaimers are repeatedly noted (e.g., Miami Gazette, Not Allowed To). The page flags hidden disclaimers as a factor that makes satire deceptive or misread as real news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-labeling versus impersonation (impostor sites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes sites that label themselves as parody/satire from impostor sites that mimic legitimate outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Parody/satire site, per PolitiFact' vs 'Impostor site, per PolitiFact' and 'Spoof of DeadState'. Impostor behavior (mimicking real outlets) is an indicator that content may be deceptive rather than clearly satirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of literary techniques typical for satire
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of understanding of literary techniques typically used for satire, such as sarcasm, irony and exaggeration, can cause readers to mistake satire for real news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snopes' list of techniques (sarcasm, irony, exaggeration) is presented as explanatory; presence of these techniques supports a classification as satire, but their subtlety can cause misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual display and excerpting (out-of-context sharing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical content being shown out of context in e-mails, memes and social media posts can lead to misperception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should check whether a snippet or image has been separated from the full article; out-of-context presentation is a common mechanism that makes satire appear factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete consumption (content not seen in full)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical content not being seen in full contributes to misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers or downstream sharers who do not read the entire article may miss satirical cues located later in a piece; completeness of reading is thus relevant when judging whether content is satire or being misread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and frame-of-reference effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Different satirical techniques appeal to different audiences; different readers have different frames of reference and some readers may not expect to see satirical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification should account for target audience and cultural/temporal references; what is obviously satirical to one group may be plausibly true to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party fact-checker classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Many entries are labeled 'Parody/satire site, per PolitiFact', 'per Snopes', or 'per FactCheck.org'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of a site in an authoritative fact-checker's list is used as evidence/criterion for labeling a site as satire or fake-news; the page relies on these external classifications heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network affiliation and shared ownership indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites are often noted as 'Possibly part of same network' or 'Part of the same network as ...', and some share owners or server details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared infrastructure (same owner, same AdSense ID, same server) or repeated cross-posting across a cluster of domains is used to infer networks that produce and amplify satirical/fake content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared AdSense ID / hidden owner information
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the same AdSense ID as Southend News Network; owner information is hidden for some sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical metadata (AdSense IDs, server hosts, WHOIS/owner info) can indicate shared control or deliberate opacity—signals of coordinated networks or deceptive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive satire indicators (clickbait, partisan appeals, ad saturation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some websites self-labeled as satire have been accused of duplicity by means of clickbait headlines, humorless appeals to partisans, hidden disclaimers, and oversaturation of ads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page highlights these behaviors as making 'satire' effectively deceptive: look for clickbait headline strategies, partisan-targeted content, disclaimers placed to minimize detection, and heavy ad monetization as red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication, copying, and republishing behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites have copied or republished stories from other fake-news outlets ('Copied story from World News Daily Report', 'Republished a story from Empire Herald').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republishing and duplication across domains (sometimes with small edits) is an indicator of networks that propagate hoaxes and may be used to assess provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virality and being mistaken as real (impact as signal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of this website's fake news hoaxes were widely shared on social media; its stories have been mistaken as real-news then shared and cited as real-news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High virality and documented cases of readers or other outlets treating content as factual are used in the page to justify a site's inclusion on the list and serve as an impact-based signal of deceptive potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status labels (active / defunct / possibly part of network)
rubrics_metrics.description: The table records site status such as 'Active' or 'Defunct' and notes when a site is 'Possibly part of same network'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational status and network suspicion are metadata used to characterize sites; status can change and is relevant for current risk assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit fictional disclaimers claiming all content is fictional
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sites' disclaimers state content is fiction (e.g., 'All characters appearing in the articles in this website—even those based on real people—are entirely fictional').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit fiction statement in an About/Disclaimer page is strong evidence the site intends satire/fiction; however, the page notes authors sometimes still defend stories as truth despite such disclaimers.
